summary: SIP is often used to reach services such as voicemail and interactive voice response systems. This document describes a convention for forming SIP service URIs that ask for a particular service when a call is redirected to such an application. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A way to write a phone address so it says not only who to call but which button to press, such as leave a message.

questions: sip uri target and cause parameters
how does sip redirect to voicemail
subtitle: Two SIP URI parameters, target and cause, tell a voicemail or IVR system which mailbox to use and why the call arrived.

tldr.problem: When a SIP call is redirected to a voicemail or similar system, that system needs to know which mailbox to use and why the call was redirected, but there was no common way to express this.
tldr.mechanism: The redirecting proxy or endpoint puts a target parameter (the mailbox) and a cause parameter (a SIP status code such as 486 for busy) into the SIP URI sent to the application.
tldr.outcome: The convention is Informational and is updated by RFC 8119. It works only when the proxy is configured to know the application supports it, and the RFC points to History-Info for the limitations.

today: RFC 4458 is Informational and is updated by RFC 8119. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: The Voicemail Addressing Problem
sections.content:
Unified Messaging (UM) and Interactive Voice Response (IVR) systems grew out of traditional telephony. When a SIP call is routed to one, the application needs to know which mailbox to use and why the call arrived, because many voicemail systems play different greetings depending on whether the user was busy or did not answer.

All this information can already travel in SIP signaling, but there was no convention for expressing it. Having every vendor make it configurable is, in the RFC's words, unrealistic for interoperability between call control, gateway and messaging systems from different vendors. The problem is harder when a gateway to a Time Division Multiplexing (TDM) network is involved, because the gateway needs both the subscriber's mailbox identifier and the number of the voicemail system.

The To header cannot simply carry the mailbox. Call control proxies cannot modify it, and the calling User Agent often sets it incorrectly because routing translates the URI several times before it reaches a name the UM system understands.
sections.eli5: An answering machine needs to know whose messages to take and which greeting to play. Without a standard way to write that down, every company would invent its own, and phones from different makers would not understand each other.

sections.title: The target and cause Parameters
sections.content:
The information is encoded in the SIP Request-URI sent to the UM system. The user and host parts identify the voicemail service, the target parameter names the mailbox, and the cause parameter gives the SIP status code that caused the retargeting. The RFC's example is sip:voicemail@example.com;target=bob%40example.com;cause=486.

target is the address of the retargeting entity. For a voicemail system on the PSTN, the user part holds the voicemail system's phone number and the target holds the subscriber's mailbox number. cause indicates the service the receiving User Agent Server should perform. The defined values are 404 (unknown or not available), 486 (user busy), 408 (no reply), 302 (unconditional), 487 (deflection during alerting), 480 (deflection immediate response) and 503 (mobile subscriber not reachable).

The names come from the ITU-T Q.732.2-5 Redirecting Reasons so that the values map to PSTN signaling. A cause with no match in a network is mapped to 302 Unconditional. The grammar is simply target-param = "target" EQUAL pvalue and cause-param = "cause" EQUAL Status-Code, and characters such as @ must be escaped in the target value. The UM system MAY treat a From header equal to the target as a hint that the user wants to retrieve messages.
sections.eli5: The address gets two extra labels. One says whose mailbox, the other says why you were sent there, using a number such as 486 for busy.

sections.title: Worked Call Flows
sections.content:
The RFC gives call flows showing where the parameters appear. In the first, Alice calls Bob, Bob's proxy sees a 486 Busy Here, and the proxy sends a new INVITE to the voicemail system whose URI carries target and cause=486. In another, Bob's phone itself answers with a 302 Moved Temporarily whose Contact URI carries the same parameters, so Alice's call is redirected straight to the voicemail.

A TDM variant puts the voicemail's phone number in the user part, for example +15555552000, and the subscriber in the target as tel:+15555551002, so a gateway can pass both to the PSTN. A zero-configuration case puts Bob's email address in the target and adds a play parameter from the Netann specification giving a greeting to fetch, and a voicexml parameter could name a script to run. A call coverage example forwards a helpdesk call to voicemail with cause=302.

The RFC says the examples are for readability only: URIs are broken across lines, some characters are not escaped, and sip: with UDP is shown although sips: with TLS is preferable.
sections.eli5: If Bob is busy, the phone company hands Alice's call to Bob's answering machine along with a note saying "this is Bob's box, and he was busy".

sections.title: Limitations and Request History
sections.content:
The proxy must know whether the UM system understands these parameters, and today that knowledge comes from configuration. The approach is therefore unlikely to work when the proxy has no such configuration or when the UM system is in a different administrative domain. It also only works for fairly simple services; it cannot say, for instance, not to offer the target's colleague because that address has already been tried.

The RFC says these limits are addressed by History-Info ( RFC 4244 ), which records the initial Request-URI and each retarget-to URI as a request is forwarded. The two can be used together: a proxy that inserts a URI with these parameters can also add a History-Info entry containing them, so the UAS can find them there even if a downstream proxy replaces the Request-URI.
sections.eli5: This works only if the phone company already knows your answering machine speaks this language, and only for simple requests. A longer trail of notes, called History-Info, can carry more detail.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
These parameters travel from a proxy to a UM system or gateway, so they must be integrity protected, otherwise an attacker could for example send a voicemail meant for a company's CEO to the attacker's mailbox. The RFC says implementations should implement and use TLS, as described in RFC 3261. The signaling also reveals who is calling whom and perhaps whether a user answered or was sent to voicemail, which encryption of the proxy-to-UM traffic can hide.

The RFC also discusses the trust problem of call forwarding: A calls B but ends up talking to C, which can look like a man-in-the-middle attack. One answer is hop-by-hop trust enforced with SIPS URIs and TLS, which still fails if a hop is untrustworthy. For callers or forwarders who want privacy, the call must go through an anonymization service such as the one in RFC 3323, and any service performing the Privacy Header function must remove the cause and target parameters from the URI.
sections.eli5: If a bad person changed the note on a call, a private message could land in the wrong mailbox. So the note must be sent over a protected line, and anyone hiding who is calling must also erase these labels.
